docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram illustrates the electrical architecture and control connections of my subsystem for the automated garment-folding device. The subsystem is responsible for controlling a linear actuator that moves one of the folding panels during the folding sequence.

The design incorporates a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller, a Fairchild Semiconductor FAN8011N H-bridge motor driver, a SKYSHALO linear actuator, a pushbutton, a status LED, a power regulation system, and connectors for communication with other team subsystems.

docs.title: Block Diagram
docs.text: Figure 1: Individual subsystem block diagram showing the microcontroller, actuator control, power distribution, user input, and subsystem connections.

docs.title: Design Decisions and System Architecture
docs.text:
The subsystem was organized around the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano because it provides digital input and output capabilities for controlling the actuator and interfacing with other components.

The FAN8011N H-bridge was selected to provide bidirectional motor control. The microcontroller sends digital control signals to the motor driver, which is intended to extend and retract the SKYSHALO linear actuator.

The power system separates the 12 V supply required by the actuator from the regulated 5 V supply used by the low-voltage electronics. A voltage regulator provides the lower-voltage supply, while a shared ground provides a common electrical reference.

A pushbutton provides a digital input, and a status LED provides visual feedback. Two subsystem connectors allow electrical connections with other parts of the team's garment-folding device.

docs.title: Microcontroller Connections
docs.text:
The block diagram identifies the following GPIO signals:

GPIO Function Signal Type RD1 Status LED Digital Output RA7 Pushbutton Digital Input RF0 H-Bridge Extend Control Digital Output RF1 H-Bridge Retract Control Digital Output RA1 Subsystem Connector 1 Digital I/O RA2 Subsystem Connector 2 Digital I/O

The connections shown represent the planned subsystem interfaces and will be verified during hardware integration and testing.

docs.title: Relationship to Product Requirements
docs.text:
The subsystem supports the automated garment-folding device by providing controlled movement of a folding panel. Bidirectional actuator operation allows the panel to move through the folding sequence and return toward its original position.

The pushbutton provides a simple user interface, while the status LED allows the user to observe system activity. The connectors support integration with the other team members' subsystems.

The separation of motor power and logic power supports the different electrical requirements of the actuator and microcontroller.

docs.title: Automated Garment Folding Device
docs.text: This report compares major components for an automated garment-folding device controlled by the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller. Components are evaluated based on affordability, performance, reliability, and compatibility with the overall design.

docs.title: 1. Linear Actuator
docs.text: The linear actuator is responsible for pushing the folding panel to fold clothing. The desired stroke length is between 4 and 8 inches, with a preferred operating voltage of 12V DC and a target cost of $30 or less per actuator.

docs.title: Option 1: VEVOR 12V High-Speed Linear Actuator
docs.text:
• Model: OK648-1000N
  • Price: $36.90
  • Voltage: 12V DC
  • Stroke: 6 inches
  • Speed: 0.55 inches/second
  • Rated force: 1000 N
  • Product: VEVOR Linear Actuator
Pros Cons Faster movement than the slower 6-inch option Exceeds the $30 budget Meets the preferred 6-inch stroke Requires an external motor driver High force capacity More force than may be needed IP54 protection Higher power demand

docs.title: Option 2: SKYSHALO 12V Linear Actuator
docs.text:
• Model: JQXXXZXQ6INCFHA2PV9-0110
  • Price: $22.22
  • Voltage: 12V DC
  • Stroke: 6 inches
  • Speed: 0.19 inches/second
  • Rated force: 1500 N
  • Product: SKYSHALO Linear Actuator
Pros Cons Within the $30 budget Slower extension speed Meets the preferred 6-inch stroke May increase folding cycle time High load capacity Requires an external motor driver Includes mounting hardware Technical documentation must be verified

docs.title: Option 3: KFFKFF 12V High-Speed Linear Actuator
docs.text:
• Price: $28.99
  • Voltage: 12V DC
  • Stroke: 4 inches
  • Speed: 0.6 inches/second
  • Rated force: 1000 N
  • Product: KFFKFF Linear Actuator
Pros Cons Within the $30 budget Shorter stroke than other options Fastest advertised movement May require different mounting geometry Suitable for compact folding mechanisms Requires an external motor driver Operates at 12V DC Technical documentation must be verified

docs.title: Final Component Selection
docs.text:
Choice: Option 3 - KFFKFF 12V High-Speed Linear Actuator (Provisional)

Rationale:

The KFFKFF linear actuator is the preferred candidate because it provides a good balance between affordability and operating speed. At approximately $28.99, it meets the project's target budget of $30 per actuator. Its advertised speed of 0.6 inches per second is faster than the other two candidates, potentially reducing the time required to fold clothing.

Although its 4-inch stroke is shorter than the other options, it may provide sufficient travel when connected to a properly designed folding-panel linkage. The final selection will depend on verifying the required mechanical movement, electrical current, and manufacturer specifications.

If a longer stroke is necessary, the SKYSHALO 6-inch actuator is the preferred budget alternative.

docs.title: 2. Photoresistor
docs.text: The photoresistor will detect changes in light caused by clothing covering the folding surface. The sensor will be connected to the PIC18F57Q43 analog input through a voltage divider.

docs.text:
• Brand: Smraza
  • Cost to team: $0.00 (provided)
  • Type: Light-dependent resistor (LDR)
  • Part number: To be confirmed
  • Purpose: Detect changes in light
Pros Cons Already available at no cost Exact specifications need verification Simple interface using a voltage divider Requires calibration No additional shipping or purchasing Sensitive to changes in ambient lighting

Product image: Add photo of our Smraza sensor.

docs.text:
• Part number: 161
  • Price: $0.95
  • Type: CdS light-dependent resistor
  • Product: Adafruit Photoresistor
Pros Cons Low purchase cost Additional purchase required Documentation and tutorials available Sensitive to ambient lighting Easy to interface with the PIC ADC Requires a voltage divider Compact size Not suitable for precise light measurements

docs.title: Option 3: SparkFun Mini Photocell
docs.text:
• Part number: SEN-09088
  • Price: $1.75
  • Light resistance: Approximately 1 kOhm
  • Dark resistance: Approximately 10 kOhm
  • Maximum power: 100 mW
  • Product: SparkFun Mini Photocell
Pros Cons Small size for installation More expensive than Adafruit option Datasheet and hookup guide available Requires additional purchase Compatible with analog sensing circuits Requires calibration for reliable detection Simple through-hole connections Affected by surrounding lighting conditions

docs.title: Final Photoresistor Selection
docs.text:
Choice: Option 1 - Smraza Photoresistor (Provisional)

Rationale:

The Smraza photoresistor is the preferred option because it is already available to our team at no additional cost. This reduces project expenses and allows immediate testing. A photoresistor can detect changes in light when clothing covers the sensing area, providing a simple input for the folding system.

The sensor can be connected to the PIC18F57Q43 using a voltage divider and analog-to-digital conversion. Before finalizing the selection, the team will verify the sensor's specifications and test its reliability under different lighting conditions.

docs.title: 3. Motor Driver (H-Bridge)
docs.text:
The motor driver will control the extension and retraction of the linear actuator in our automated garment-folding device. The PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller will send control signals to the motor driver, which will control the direction of the actuator's DC motor.

The motor driver must support bidirectional operation and handle the electrical current required by the selected actuator.

docs.title: Option 1: FAN8011N H-Bridge
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: Fairchild Semiconductor
  • Model: FAN8011N
  • Cost to team: $0.00 (provided in class)
  • Type: Motor driver integrated circuit
  • Operating voltage: Must be verified using the datasheet
  • Output current: Must be verified
  • Product information: FAN8011N Datasheet Search
Pros Cons Already available at no additional cost Output current must be verified No additional purchasing required May require external circuitry Designed for motor-control applications Compatibility with our actuator is not yet confirmed Can be incorporated into our custom PCB Requires careful circuit design and testing

docs.title: Option 2: L298N Motor Driver Module
docs.text:
• Model: L298N
  • Estimated price: \(4-\)10
  • Motor supply voltage: Up to 46V (IC rating)
  • Output current: Up to 2A per channel (IC rating)
  • Type: Dual H-bridge motor driver
  • Product information: L298N Datasheet
Pros Cons Affordable and widely available Significant voltage drop during operation Supports forward and reverse motor control Less efficient than newer motor drivers Compatible with microcontroller control signals Current capability may be insufficient Commonly used in educational projects May require heatsinking under load

docs.title: Option 3: Pololu VNH5019 Motor Driver
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: Pololu
  • Model: VNH5019 Motor Driver Carrier
  • Approximate price: $20
  • Operating voltage: 5.5V to 24V
  • Continuous current capability: Approximately 12A under suitable cooling conditions
  • Type: High-current H-bridge motor driver
  • Product: Pololu VNH5019
Pros Cons Designed for higher-current DC motors More expensive than the other options Supports bidirectional motor control Additional purchase required Includes current-sensing capability Larger board than a single IC Includes protection features Must still be checked against motor stall current

docs.title: Final Motor Driver Selection
docs.text:
Choice: Option 1 - FAN8011N H-Bridge (Provisional)

Rationale:

The FAN8011N is our initial preferred motor-driver candidate because it was provided in class at no additional cost. Using an available component would reduce our project expenses and allow us to integrate the motor-control circuit into our existing hardware design.

However, the FAN8011N must be evaluated against the selected linear actuator's voltage and current requirements before the selection can be finalized.

The L298N offers an inexpensive alternative, but its limited current capability and electrical losses may reduce performance.

The Pololu VNH5019 provides a higher-current alternative with additional protection and monitoring features, making it a stronger choice if our actuator requires more current than the class-provided driver can safely deliver.

The final motor-driver selection will be based on verified electrical compatibility, reliability, and overall cost.

docs.title: 4. Power Supply and Power Input
docs.text:
The automated garment-folding device requires electrical power for its linear actuator, motor driver, microcontroller, and sensors.

Three power-delivery approaches are considered: a wall-connected power supply, two 9V batteries connected in series, and an external DC supply connected through a barrel jack.

docs.title: Option 1: Wall-Connected AC/DC Power Supply
docs.text:
• Example model: MEAN WELL GST60A12-P1J
  • Input: Household AC electricity
  • Output: 12V DC
  • Maximum output current: 5A
  • Rated power: 60W
  • Price: Verify current vendor price
  • Product: MEAN WELL GST60A12-P1J
Pros Cons Provides continuous power from a wall outlet Requires access to an electrical outlet Regulated 12V output Not portable Enclosed power adapter Output current must meet actuator requirements Suitable for household operation Additional regulation needed for low-voltage electronics

docs.title: Option 2: Two 9V Batteries Connected in Series
docs.text:
• Example: Two Energizer MAX 9V alkaline batteries
  • Battery voltage: 9V each
  • Combined nominal voltage: 18V DC
  • Configuration: Series connection
  • Price: Cost of two batteries and battery connectors
  • Datasheet: Energizer 9V Battery
Pros Cons Portable power source 18V is too high for a 12V actuator without regulation Does not require a wall outlet Poor choice for high-current motor loads Simple battery connections Batteries require replacement Useful for low-power experiments Limited runtime and voltage stability

docs.title: Option 3: External DC Supply Through a Barrel Jack
docs.text:
• Connector: Three-pin DC barrel jack
  • Cost to team: $0.00 (provided in class)
  • Input voltage: Depends on connected external supply
  • Proposed supply: Regulated 12V DC adapter
  • Connector information: Pololu DC Barrel Jack
Pros Cons Barrel jack already available to the team Jack does not generate power Allows easy connection and disconnection Requires a compatible external supply Convenient for PCB integration Plug dimensions and polarity must match Can support external power during testing Current rating must be verified

docs.title: Final Power Supply Selection
docs.text:
Choice: Option 1 - Wall-Connected 12V AC/DC Supply

Rationale:

The wall-connected 12V DC power supply is the preferred option because the automated garment-folding device is intended primarily for household use.

A regulated wall adapter provides continuous power without requiring battery replacement. It also avoids the limitations of two 9V batteries, which produce approximately 18V in series and are poorly suited to high-current motor applications.

The existing barrel jack may be used as the physical connection between the wall adapter and the device, provided the connector dimensions, polarity, and current ratings are compatible.

The final supply rating will be selected after calculating the total current requirements and including a 25% safety margin.

docs.title: 5. Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
The voltage regulator converts the 12V DC power supply into a regulated 5V output for the low-voltage components of our automated garment-folding device.

Three voltage regulators are compared based on cost, efficiency, output current, heat generation, and ease of integration.

docs.title: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805ABV
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: STMicroelectronics
  • Model: L7805ABV
  • Cost to team: $0.00 (provided in class)
  • Type: Linear voltage regulator
  • Output voltage: 5V DC
  • Rated output current: Up to 1.5A with adequate cooling
  • Package: TO-220
  • Datasheet: STMicroelectronics L78 Series
Pros Cons Already available at no additional cost Generates heat when stepping 12V down to 5V Provides a fixed 5V output Less efficient than switching regulators Simple three-pin design May require a heatsink Easy to integrate into a custom PCB Current capacity depends on thermal conditions No output adjustment required Not ideal for high-current applications

docs.title: Option 2: LM2596 Adjustable Buck Converter
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: Texas Instruments (regulator IC)
  • Model: LM2596-based adjustable module
  • Type: Switching step-down regulator
  • Input voltage: Typically 4.5V to 40V for the IC
  • Output voltage: Adjustable
  • Rated IC output current: Up to 3A
  • Price: Verify selected module price
  • Product: Texas Instruments LM2596
Pros Cons Higher efficiency than a linear regulator Requires output voltage adjustment Produces less heat during voltage conversion More complex circuitry Can provide relatively high output current Switching may introduce electrical noise Suitable for 12V-to-5V conversion Module quality varies by manufacturer

docs.title: Option 3: Pololu D24V22F5
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: Pololu
  • Model: D24V22F5
  • Type: Fixed-output switching regulator
  • Input voltage: 5.3V to 36V, subject to dropout requirements
  • Output voltage: 5V DC
  • Typical maximum output current: Approximately 2.5A, depending on operating conditions
  • Approximate price: $18.95
  • Product: Pololu D24V22F5
Pros Cons High efficiency More expensive than our existing regulator Fixed 5V output Requires an additional purchase Compact size Current capacity depends on operating conditions Includes electrical protection features More complex internal design Produces less heat than a linear regulator Switching can introduce electrical noise

docs.title: Final Voltage Regulator Selection
docs.text:
Choice: Option 1 - STMicroelectronics L7805ABV (Provisional)

Rationale:

The STMicroelectronics L7805ABV is our preferred voltage regulator because it was provided in class at no additional cost. Using this component reduces the overall project budget and allows us to integrate the regulator directly into our custom circuit.

The L7805ABV provides a fixed 5V output suitable for compatible low-voltage electronic components. Its simple three-pin design also makes it easier to incorporate into our schematic and PCB.

Although the LM2596 and Pololu D24V22F5 offer higher efficiency, the L7805ABV may be sufficient for our design if the total 5V current requirement is relatively low.

The main disadvantage is heat generation when converting 12V to 5V. For example, at a load current of 0.2A:

Power dissipated = (12V - 5V) x 0.2A = 1.4W

This heat may require a heatsink or other thermal management.

Before finalizing the selection, the team will verify the total current requirement, thermal performance, and correct power connection for the PIC18F57Q43 development board.

docs.title: 6. Operational Amplifier (Op-Amp)
docs.text:
The operational amplifier may be used to condition analog signals from sensors in our automated garment-folding device. It can buffer, amplify, or filter sensor signals before they are measured by the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

Three quad operational amplifiers are compared based on cost, operating voltage, power consumption, signal performance, and ease of integration.

docs.title: Option 1: Microchip MCP6004
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: Microchip Technology
  • Model: MCP6004
  • Cost to team: $0.00 (provided in class)
  • Type: Quad operational amplifier
  • Number of amplifiers: 4
  • Operating voltage: 1.8V to 6.0V
  • Gain-bandwidth product: 1 MHz
  • Input/output: Rail-to-rail
  • Typical supply current: 100 microamps per amplifier
  • Product: Microchip MCP6004
Pros Cons Already available at no additional cost Cannot operate directly from the 12V supply Compatible with a regulated 5V supply Requires proper signal-conditioning circuitry Rail-to-rail input and output Limited 1 MHz bandwidth Low power consumption Four amplifiers may be unnecessary Four amplifiers in one IC Additional wiring and PCB space required

docs.title: Option 2: Texas Instruments LM324
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: Texas Instruments
  • Model: LM324
  • Type: Quad operational amplifier
  • Number of amplifiers: 4
  • Operating voltage: 3V to 30V
  • Gain-bandwidth product: 1.2 MHz
  • Typical supply current: 175 microamps per amplifier
  • Price: Verify current supplier price
  • Product: Texas Instruments LM324
Pros Cons Wide operating voltage range Output does not swing fully to the positive supply Four amplifiers in one IC Less suitable for full-range 5V ADC signals Common and well-documented Additional purchase required Suitable for basic analog signal processing Higher input bias current than CMOS alternatives

docs.title: Option 3: Texas Instruments TLV2374
docs.text:
• Manufacturer: Texas Instruments
  • Model: TLV2374
  • Type: Quad operational amplifier
  • Number of amplifiers: 4
  • Operating voltage: 2.7V to 16V
  • Gain-bandwidth product: 3 MHz
  • Input/output: Rail-to-rail
  • Typical supply current: 550 microamps per amplifier
  • Price: Verify current supplier price
  • Product: Texas Instruments TLV2374
Pros Cons Higher bandwidth than MCP6004 Additional purchase required Rail-to-rail input and output Higher typical supply current Compatible with a 5V supply Higher performance may be unnecessary Four amplifiers in one IC Requires external circuit components

docs.title: Final Operational Amplifier Selection
docs.text:
Choice: Option 1 - Microchip MCP6004 (Provisional)

Rationale:

The Microchip MCP6004 is our preferred operational amplifier because it was provided in class at no additional cost. Its low power consumption and compatibility with a regulated 5V supply make it suitable for our embedded system.

The MCP6004 provides four independent operational amplifiers, allowing multiple analog signals to be conditioned if necessary. Its rail-to-rail input and output capability is useful for interfacing with the microcontroller's analog-to-digital converter.

Although the TLV2374 offers greater bandwidth and the LM324 supports a wider supply voltage range, the MCP6004 provides sufficient performance for many low-frequency sensor applications without requiring an additional purchase.

The final circuit will be evaluated to determine whether amplification or buffering is necessary. If the photoresistor can be read reliably using a simple voltage divider, the operational amplifier may not be required for that sensor.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This Bill of Materials (BOM) documents the electrical, electromechanical, and mechanical components required for the automated garment-folding subsystem. It establishes the component inventory, design requirements, and estimated procurement costs for prototype development and system integration.

The subsystem incorporates a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller, a 12V linear actuator, an H-bridge motor driver, voltage regulation, circuit protection, and electrical connectors. Additional mechanical components include 3D-printed supports and hinges for the folding mechanism.

The BOM was developed from the KiCad schematic and component selection process.

docs.title: Bill of Materials
docs.text:
The following figure presents the completed Bill of Materials, including component descriptions, quantities, pricing, and purchasing information recorded in the Excel spreadsheet.

Figure 1: Bill of Materials for the automated garment-folding subsystem.

docs.title: Microcontroller
docs.text:
The Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano serves as the subsystem controller. It provides digital input/output functionality for actuator control, user inputs, status indication, and communication with other team subsystems.

The development board was selected for compatibility with MPLAB X IDE, MCC Melody, and the team's embedded development environment.

docs.title: Motor Driver and Linear Actuator
docs.text:
The folding mechanism uses a SKYSHALO 12V linear actuator with a nominal 6-inch stroke. The actuator provides the mechanical force required to extend and retract the folding panel.

The FAN8011N H-bridge is identified in the schematic for bidirectional motor control. Its suitability for the actuator must be confirmed against operating current, stall current, and driver output ratings before hardware implementation.

docs.title: Mechanical Components
docs.text:
The subsystem incorporates 3D-printed structural components and folding-panel hinges.

PLA or PETG filament supports fabrication of custom mounting brackets, actuator supports, and structural attachments. Hinges allow the folding panel to rotate relative to the stationary platform.

These components provide mechanical flexibility and allow modifications during prototype testing.

docs.title: Power Regulation and Protection
docs.text:
The subsystem uses a 12V DC supply for actuator operation and an L7805 regulator for the 5V control circuitry.

Input protection is provided by a fuse. The final fuse rating must be coordinated with actuator current requirements, conductor ratings, and expected startup conditions.

docs.title: User Input and Status Indication
docs.text:
A momentary pushbutton provides a digital control input, while an LED indicates subsystem status.

The circuit incorporates current-limiting and pull-up resistors along with capacitors for regulation stability and input signal conditioning.

docs.title: Connectors and System Integration
docs.text:
The subsystem includes 8-pin, 4-pin, and 2-pin electrical connectors for interfacing with external components and other team subsystems.

Connector selection considers pin count, physical compatibility, current capacity, and ease of assembly. Matching connector interfaces are required for reliable integration.

docs.title: Cost Analysis
docs.text:
The component prices and quantities documented in Figure 1 provide the basis for estimating subsystem procurement costs.

The BOM includes electronic components, actuator hardware, connectors, and mechanical fabrication materials. Components already available through laboratory inventory may reduce the actual purchasing cost.

Additional quantities should be considered for breadboard prototyping, PCB assembly, and replacement parts. The final purchase request will distinguish existing inventory from components requiring procurement.

docs.title: Relationship to Product Requirements
docs.text:
The selected components support controlled folding-panel movement, subsystem integration, and prototype reliability.

The linear actuator and hinges provide the mechanical folding action, while the microcontroller and motor driver coordinate electrical control. The modular connectors support integration with other team subsystems.

The design prioritizes functional performance, affordability, maintainability, and ease of prototype modification.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The Bill of Materials establishes the component requirements for manufacturing, assembling, and testing the automated garment-folding subsystem.

The completed spreadsheet provides a reference for component selection, purchasing decisions, and cost tracking. Final hardware verification will focus on actuator-driver compatibility, power protection, connector interfaces, and mechanical assembly requirements.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic illustrates the electrical design of the linear actuator control subsystem for our automated garment-folding machine. The subsystem uses a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller to control a 12 V linear actuator through a Fairchild Semiconductor FAN8011N H-bridge motor driver.

The linear actuator is responsible for moving one of the folding panels. The H-bridge allows the microcontroller to control the actuator's direction of movement, enabling the panel to extend and retract during the folding sequence.

docs.title: Microcontroller and Motor Control
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano serves as the subsystem controller. Digital control signals are sent to the FAN8011N H-bridge, which switches the motor output polarity to extend or retract the linear actuator.

The H-bridge separates the low-power microcontroller control signals from the higher-power actuator circuit.

docs.title: Power Supply
docs.text:
The circuit includes a DC barrel jack, fuse, and L7805 voltage regulator. The regulator provides a regulated 5 V supply for the appropriate low-voltage components, while the actuator requires a 12 V power source.

The fuse provides protection against excessive current. The motor driver and power supply must be appropriately rated for the actuator's operating and stall currents.

docs.title: User Input and Status Indicator
docs.text:
A pushbutton provides a digital input to the microcontroller through RA7. The button circuit includes a 10 kΩ resistor and a 0.1 µF capacitor to establish a stable input and reduce unwanted switching noise.

A status LED with a 330 Ω current-limiting resistor provides visual feedback during subsystem operation.

docs.title: Electrical Connections
docs.text:
The schematic includes an eight-pin connector for communication and interfacing with other subsystems, a four-pin connector, and a two-pin connector for the linear actuator.

These connections allow the subsystem to be integrated into the complete automated folding machine.

docs.title: Product Requirements
docs.text:
This subsystem supports the product requirements by providing controlled folding-panel movement, a user-operated input, and an electrical interface for communication with the other subsystems.

The linear actuator provides the mechanical motion required to fold garments, while the microcontroller coordinates actuator operation as part of the overall folding sequence.
